summary.text: The cases \(n=2,3,4\) follow from \(a(9)=9\) and digit-congruence arguments for 3- and 9-digit candidates: divisibility of both a number and its reversal by \(27\) or \(81\) forces its digit sum to be divisible by the same modulus, so positivity and the maximal possible digit sum force the first candidate to be \(999\) or \(999999999\). For \(n\ge5\), the palindrome obtained by repeating the block \(68899199886\) (once up to \(n=11\), and \(3^{n-12}\) times thereafter) is divisible by \(3^n\); a geometric-sum factorization supplies each additional factor of 3, while its \(11\cdot3^{n-12}\) digits make it strictly smaller than the corresponding all-nines number.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\operatorname{rev}(m)\) denote the integer obtained by reversing the decimal digits of \(m\), with any zeros that become leading zeros discarded. For a positive integer \(N\), the number \(a(N)\) is the least positive multiple \(kN\) such that \(N\mid \operatorname{rev}(kN)\), if such a multiple exists.

We prove that, for every \(n\ge 2\),
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\in\{2,3,4\}.
\]

We first record a simple consequence of the definition. If \(m>0\), \(N\mid m\), and \(N\mid\operatorname{rev}(m)\), then
\[
a(N)\le m.
\]
Indeed, write \(m=kN\). Since \(m>0\), we have \(k>0\), so \(k\) is one of the admissible multipliers among which the defining minimum is taken.

The proof has two parts. First we determine \(a(9),a(27),a(81)\). Then we construct, for every \(n\ge5\), an admissible multiple of \(3^n\) smaller than the proposed all-nines number.

----------------------------------------------------------------
1. A digit congruence
----------------------------------------------------------------

For a finite list of digits
\[
D=(d_0,d_1,\dots,d_{r-1}),
\]
written in least-significant-digit-first order, put
\[
F_b(D)=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}d_i b^i,
\qquad
S(D)=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}d_i.
\]
Thus \(F_{10}(D)\) is the number represented by \(D\), and
\[
F_{10}(D^{\mathrm{rev}})=\sum_{i=0}^{r-1}d_i10^{r-1-i}.
\]

The number \(73\) is useful because
\[
10\cdot73=730\equiv1\pmod{81}.
\]
Consequently, for every digit list of length \(r\),
\[
10F_{10}(D^{\mathrm{rev}})
\equiv 10^rF_{73}(D)\pmod{81}. \tag{1}
\]
To see this term by term, the coefficient of \(d_i\) on the left is \(10^{r-i}\), while that on the right is \(10^r73^i\); and
\[
10^r73^i=10^{r-i}(10\cdot73)^i\equiv10^{r-i}\pmod{81}.
\]
The same identity may of course be reduced modulo \(27\).

For a list of exactly nine digits, \(10^9\equiv10\cdot73\pmod{81}\). Substituting this into (1), and cancelling \(10\), which is coprime to \(81\), gives
\[
F_{10}(D^{\mathrm{rev}})\equiv73F_{73}(D)\pmod{81}
\qquad (|D|=9). \tag{2}
\]
Likewise, if \(|D|=3\), then modulo \(27\) we have
\(10^3\equiv10\cdot73\), so cancellation of \(10\) gives
\[
F_{10}(D^{\mathrm{rev}})\equiv73F_{73}(D)\pmod{27}
\qquad (|D|=3). \tag{3}
\]

We also need a digit-sum congruence. For a list of at most nine digits,
\[
F_{10}(D)+73F_{73}(D)\equiv74S(D)\pmod{81}. \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, the coefficient of \(d_i\) on the left is
\(10^i+73^{i+1}\). For \(0\le i\le8\), the two residues modulo \(81\) are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}
i&0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\ \hline
10^i&1&10&19&28&37&46&55&64&73\\
73^{i+1}&73&64&55&46&37&28&19&10&1
\end{array}
\]
Every column sums to \(74\) modulo \(81\), proving (4). Reducing (4) modulo \(27\) gives the corresponding congruence modulo \(27\) for lists of at most three digits (and in fact for all lists of at most nine digits).

These congruences imply the following useful fact.

**Nine-digit consequence.** Suppose \(D\) consists of nine decimal digits, and both \(F_{10}(D)\) and \(F_{10}(D^{\mathrm{rev}})\) are divisible by \(81\). By (2), divisibility of the reversed value implies
\[
81\mid73F_{73}(D).
\]
Since \(\gcd(73,81)=1\), it follows that \(81\mid F_{73}(D)\). Equation (4) then yields
\[
81\mid74S(D).
\]
As \(\gcd(74,81)=1\), we conclude
\[
81\mid S(D). \tag{5}
\]
Because there are nine digits and each is between \(0\) and \(9\),
\[
0\le S(D)\le81.
\]
Thus (5) forces \(S(D)=0\) or \(S(D)=81\). In the first case all nine digits are zero. In the second case all nine digits are nine, because \(81\) is the maximum possible sum of nine decimal digits.

Exactly the same argument with (3), (4) reduced modulo \(27\), and the coprimalities
\[
\gcd(73,27)=\gcd(74,27)=1
\]
gives the following three-digit consequence: if \(D\) consists of three decimal digits and both \(F_{10}(D)\) and \(F_{10}(D^{\mathrm{rev}})\) are divisible by \(27\), then \(27\mid S(D)\). Since \(0\le S(D)\le27\), either all three digits are zero or all three are nine.

----------------------------------------------------------------
2. The exact values at \(9,27,81\)
----------------------------------------------------------------

Clearly \(9\) is divisible by \(9\), and its reversal is again \(9\). There is no smaller positive multiple of \(9\). Hence
\[
a(9)=9. \tag{6}
\]

Next, \(999=37\cdot27\), and its reversal is itself. We claim there is no smaller admissible positive multiple of \(27\). Suppose, to the contrary, that
\[
m=j\cdot27,
\qquad 0<j<37,
\]
and \(27\mid\operatorname{rev}(m)\). Then \(0<m<999<10^3\).

Write the decimal digits of \(m\) least-significant first, and append zeros at the high-digit end until the list has exactly three entries. Call the resulting list \(D\). Then \(F_{10}(D)=m\). Reversing this padded list merely inserts some zeros at the low-digit end of the reversed unpadded list. Consequently
\[
F_{10}(D^{\mathrm{rev}})=10^q\operatorname{rev}(m)
\]
for some \(q\ge0\), and is therefore divisible by \(27\). Since \(m\) itself is divisible by \(27\), the three-digit consequence above says that either every digit of \(D\) is zero or every digit is nine. The first possibility contradicts \(m>0\); the second gives \(m=999\), contradicting \(m<999\). Thus no such \(m\) exists, and
\[
a(27)=999. \tag{7}
\]

Similarly,
\[
999999999=12345679\cdot81,
\]
and this number is its own reversal. We show that there is no smaller admissible positive multiple of \(81\). Suppose
\[
m=j\cdot81,
\qquad 0<j<12345679,
\]
and \(81\mid\operatorname{rev}(m)\). Then
\[
0<m<999999999<10^9.
\]
Pad the least-significant-first decimal digit list of \(m\) with high-end zeros to obtain a list \(D\) of exactly nine digits. As before,
\[
F_{10}(D)=m,
\qquad
F_{10}(D^{\mathrm{rev}})=10^q\operatorname{rev}(m)

to some \(q\ge0\). Both are divisible by \(81\). The nine-digit consequence says that either all nine digits are zero or all are nine. The first option contradicts \(m>0\); the second gives \(m=999999999\), contradicting the strict inequality. Therefore
\[
a(81)=999999999. \tag{8}
\]

Equations (6)--(8) already prove the desired equality for the three claimed exponents:
\[
\begin{aligned}
n=2:&\quad a(3^2)=a(9)=9=10^{3^0}-1,\\
n=3:&\quad a(3^3)=a(27)=999=10^{3^1}-1,\\
n=4:&\quad a(3^4)=a(81)=999999999=10^{3^2}-1.
\end{aligned} \tag{9}
\]

----------------------------------------------------------------
3. Palindromic witnesses for every \(n\ge5\)
----------------------------------------------------------------

Consider the eleven-digit palindrome
\[
B=68899199886.
\]
A direct division gives
\[
B=3^{12}\cdot129646. \tag{10}
\]
For \(t\ge1\), form the number consisting of \(t\) consecutive copies of this eleven-digit block:
\[
P_t=B\bigl(1+10^{11}+10^{22}+\cdots+10^{11(t-1)}\bigr). \tag{11}
\]
Since the block \(68899199886\) is a palindrome and all the repeated blocks are identical, \(P_t\) is also a palindrome. Thus
\[
\operatorname{rev}(P_t)=P_t. \tag{12}
\]
Also, \(P_t\) has \(11t\) decimal digits, so in particular
\[
0<P_t<10^{11t}. \tag{13}
\]

Set
\[
Q=10^{11},
\qquad
R_t=1+Q+Q^2+\cdots+Q^{t-1}.
\]
Thus \(P_t=BR_t\). We claim that for every \(k\ge0\),
\[
3^k\mid R_{3^k}. \tag{14}
\]
This follows by induction on \(k\). For \(k=0\), \(R_1=1\), so the assertion is immediate. For any \(t\), splitting the sum into three blocks gives
\[
R_{3t}=R_t\bigl(1+Q^t+Q^{2t}\bigr). \tag{15}
\]
Because \(Q=10^{11}\equiv1\pmod3\), the second factor in (15) satisfies
\[
1+Q^t+Q^{2t}\equiv1+1+1\equiv0\pmod3.
\]
Hence, if \(3^k\mid R_{3^k}\), equation (15) with \(t=3^k\) shows that \(3^{k+1}\mid R_{3^{k+1}}\). This proves (14).

We now split the exponents \(n\ge5\) into two ranges.

### The range \(5\le n<12\)

By (10), \(3^{12}\mid B\), and therefore \(3^n\mid B\). Since \(B\) is a positive palindrome, both \(B\) and its reversal are divisible by \(3^n\). It follows from the minimality observation that
\[
a(3^n)\le B. \tag{16}
\]
On the other hand, \(n\ge5\) implies \(n-2\ge3\), and hence
\[
3^{n-2}\ge3^3=27.
\]
The numerical inequality
\[
B=68899199886<10^{27}-1
\]
therefore gives
\[
B<10^{3^{n-2}}-1. \tag{17}
\]
Combining (16) and (17),
\[
a(3^n)<10^{3^{n-2}}-1,
\]
so equality is impossible throughout this range.

### The range \(n\ge12\)

Write
\[
k=n-12,
\qquad
t=3^k.
\]
By (10), \(3^{12}\mid B\), and by (14), \(3^k\mid R_t\). Therefore
\[
3^n=3^{12+k}\mid BR_t=P_t. \tag{18}
\]
Because \(P_t\) is a palindrome, (12) and (18) show that its reversal is divisible by \(3^n\) as well. Hence
\[
a(3^n)\le P_t. \tag{19}
\]

It remains to compare its size with the proposed all-nines number. Since \(n=12+k\),
\[
3^{n-2}=3^{10+k}=3^{10}\,3^k=59049t.
\]
In particular,
\[
11t<3^{n-2}. \tag{20}
\]
By (13) and (20),
\[
P_t<10^{11t}<10^{3^{n-2}}.
\]
All quantities are integers, so the strict inequality \(10^{11t}<10^{3^{n-2}}\), together with \(P_t<10^{11t}\), yields the sharper bound
\[
P_t<10^{3^{n-2}}-1. \tag{21}
\]
For example, from \(P_t<10^{11t}\) we have \(P_t+1\le10^{11t}\), and (20) gives \(10^{11t}<10^{3^{n-2}}\); hence \(P_t+1<10^{3^{n-2}}\), which is exactly (21).

Combining (19) and (21), we again obtain
\[
a(3^n)<10^{3^{n-2}}-1.
\]
Thus the proposed equality fails for every \(n\ge12\), and together with the preceding range it fails for every \(n\ge5\).

----------------------------------------------------------------
4. Completion of the equivalence
----------------------------------------------------------------

We have shown in (9) that the equality holds for \(n=2,3,4\). Conversely, assume \(n\ge2\) and that \(n\notin\{2,3,4\}\). Since \(n\) is an integer, this forces \(n\ge5\). The palindromic witness argument then gives the strict inequality
\[
a(3^n)<10^{3^{n-2}}-1,
\]
so equality cannot hold. Therefore, for every integer \(n\ge2\),
\[
\boxed{
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\iff n=2\text{ or }n=3\text{ or }n=4.
}
\]
